1.summary: Haggai rebukes the people for living in panelled houses while God's house lies in ruins, links their failing harvests to this neglect, and within weeks the leaders and people begin the work.
1.lookfor: Notice the exact dates, the repeated call to consider your ways, and how quickly the people respond.

names.name: Darius
names.gloss: Darius I, king of Persia from 522 to 486 BC.

names.name: Zerubbabel
names.gloss: Governor of Judah under Persia and grandson of King Jehoiachin.

names.name: Shealtiel
names.gloss: Zerubbabel's father, a son of the exiled King Jehoiachin.

names.name: Joshua
names.gloss: The high priest of the returned community, called Jeshua in Ezra.

names.name: Jehozadak
names.gloss: Joshua's father, the high priest taken into exile in 586 BC.

insights.title: A stalled building site
insights.body: Cyrus allowed the exiles to return in 538 BC, and they laid the temple's foundation, but local opposition halted the work for years. By 520 BC little had been done. Haggai and Zechariah stirred the people to start again, and the temple was finished in 515 BC.

insights.title: Dated to the day
insights.body: Haggai's first word came on the first day of the sixth month (1:1), in late August 520 BC. The first day of the month was a new moon, when people gathered for worship. Every message in the book has an exact date, which modern scholars can match to the Babylonian calendar.

insights.title: The time hasn't come
insights.body: The people said the time had not yet come to build God's house (1:2). Perhaps they were waiting for better economic times, or thought the seventy years of Jeremiah's prophecy were not yet complete. Haggai answers that they found time to finish their own houses.

insights.title: Paneled houses
insights.body: Paneled houses (1:4) were lined with wood, a sign of comfort and wealth in a land where timber was costly. Solomon's palace and temple were panelled with cedar. The contrast is between comfortable homes and a ruined sanctuary.

insights.title: A bag with holes
insights.body: Wages put into a bag with holes (1:6) is a vivid picture of money that disappears. They sow, eat, drink and dress, but nothing is ever enough. Haggai links this to the neglect of God's house (1:9), in the language of the covenant curses.

insights.title: Consider your ways
insights.body: Consider your ways (1:5, 1:7) is literally set your heart on your ways. Haggai asks the people to look honestly at their lives and their results. The phrase returns in chapter 2 as consider from this day.

insights.title: I am with you
insights.body: When the people obey and fear Yahweh, Haggai brings a short message: I am with you (1:13). Then God stirs up the spirit of the leaders and people, and work begins 23 days later (1:14-15). Obedience and God's stirring work together.

insights.title: My house lies waste
insights.body: Haggai sees the ruined temple as a sign of misplaced priorities: each of you is busy with his own house (1:9). Christians have often applied this to the priorities of their own lives. What might it mean today to put God's house first, and what might it not mean?

2.summary: Haggai encourages the builders that the new temple's glory will surpass the old, teaches through a question to the priests that their offerings had been unclean, promises blessing from that day, and names Zerubbabel as God's chosen signet ring.
2.lookfor: Notice the feeling of the older people in 2:3, the promise to shake the nations, the priests' answers, and the final word to Zerubbabel.

names.name: Zerubbabel
names.gloss: Governor of Judah from David's royal line.

names.name: Egypt
names.gloss: Where Israel had been slaves before the exodus.

insights.title: As nothing in your eyes
insights.body: Haggai's second message came on the last day of the feast of Tabernacles (2:1), when people would remember Solomon's dedication of the first temple at the same feast. Old people who had seen Solomon's temple thought the new one was as nothing (2:3). Ezra records that they wept when its foundation was laid.

insights.title: Be strong and work
insights.body: Be strong, Zerubbabel ... Be strong, Joshua ... Be strong, all you people of the land ... and work, for I am with you (2:4). The threefold command echoes God's words to Joshua before the conquest. The promise rests on the covenant from the exodus and God's Spirit among them (2:5).

insights.title: Shaking heaven and earth
insights.body: Yet once ... I will shake the heavens, the earth, the sea, and the dry land (2:6). Darius had just put down widespread revolts across the empire, so a shaking of nations was easy to imagine. Hebrews quotes this verse to contrast created things that can be shaken with the kingdom that cannot.

insights.title: The desire of all nations
insights.body: The precious things of all nations will come (2:7). The Hebrew word, chemdat, means what is desirable or treasured. The King James Version translated it the desire of all nations and many Christians read it as a title for the Messiah; most modern translations, following the plural verb, take it as the nations' treasures, which fits the next verse.

insights.title: Greater glory
insights.body: The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former (2:9). Herod the Great later rebuilt and vastly enlarged this temple, which Jesus taught in. Christians have also seen its greater glory in Jesus's presence there, while Jewish tradition looks forward to the glory of a future temple.

insights.title: Holiness doesn't spread, impurity does
insights.body: Haggai asks the priests two questions about the law (2:11-13). Holy meat does not make other food holy by touching it, but contact with a corpse makes things unclean. His point is that the people's offerings on a ruined site had been unclean; holiness is not caught by contact with holy things.

insights.title: From today I will bless you
insights.body: On the day the foundation was relaid (2:18), God promises: From today I will bless you (2:19). The seed was not yet in the barn and the trees had not produced, so the blessing had to be trusted before it was seen. The date fell in December, after the autumn sowing.

insights.title: Zerubbabel the signet
insights.body: God will make Zerubbabel like a signet ring (2:23). A signet bore its owner's seal and authority. Jeremiah had said that even if Zerubbabel's grandfather Jehoiachin were a signet on God's hand, God would pull him off; Haggai reverses that curse on David's line. Matthew lists Zerubbabel among Jesus's ancestors.

intro.who: Haggai, a prophet among the Jews who had returned from Babylon, named alongside Zechariah in the book of Ezra. His name probably means festal, perhaps because he was born on a feast day.
intro.when: Its four messages are precisely dated between late August and mid-December 520 BC, in the second year of the Persian king Darius I, about eighteen years after the first exiles returned.
intro.why: It urges the returned community, discouraged and preoccupied with their own houses, to rebuild the temple, promising that God is with them and that its glory will surpass the old.
